questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort?
questions.explanation: All three simple comparison sorts perform on the order of n^2 comparisons in the worst case. Merge sort and heapsort improve this to O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?

options.text: It cannot crash on any input
Equal elements keep their original relative order

questions.explanation: Stability preserves the input order of records that compare equal, which matters when sorting by one key after another. Merge sort is stable; heapsort and typical quicksort are not.

questions.prompt: On an array that is already sorted, insertion sort runs in:
questions.explanation: Each element is already in place, so every inner comparison stops immediately and only n-1 comparisons are made overall. This best case makes insertion sort excellent for nearly-sorted data.

questions.prompt: What is the average-case time complexity of merge sort?
questions.explanation: The array is split log n times and each level does O(n) merging, giving O(n log n) in the best, average and worst cases. Its drawback is the O(n) auxiliary array it requires.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm always makes exactly the same number of comparisons regardless of the input order?

options.text: Bubble sort with an early-exit flag

questions.explanation: Selection sort scans the entire unsorted portion to find the minimum on every pass, so its comparison count is fixed at about n^2/2 no matter the arrangement. Its number of swaps, however, is only O(n).

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of the standard merge sort on arrays?
questions.explanation: Merging requires an auxiliary buffer the size of the input, so it uses O(n) extra space. This is the main reason an in-place algorithm like heapsort is sometimes preferred.

questions.prompt: Which simple sort is generally the best choice for small or nearly-sorted arrays?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort has low overhead and approaches O(n) on nearly-sorted input, which is why real library sorts switch to it for small subarrays. This is the idea behind hybrid sorts like Timsort.

questions.prompt: The theoretical lower bound for any comparison-based sorting algorithm is:
questions.explanation: There are n! possible orderings and each comparison distinguishes at most two branches, so at least log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) comparisons are needed. Non-comparison sorts like counting sort can beat this.

questions.prompt: Counting sort achieves O(n + k) time for n integers in the range 0 to k. What is its main limitation?

options.text: It requires the input to be sorted
It needs O(k) space and is only practical when k is not much larger than n

questions.explanation: The count array has one slot per possible value, so a huge value range makes it wasteful or infeasible. When k is comparable to n, it beats the O(n log n) comparison bound.

questions.prompt: In selection sort, how many swaps are performed in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Each of the n passes performs at most one swap to place the minimum, so there are at most n-1 swaps. This makes it attractive when writes are far more expensive than reads.
